title: The Great Wall of China
summary: Why China built and rebuilt the Great Wall over two thousand years, what it was made of, how soldiers used its towers to send signals, and the myth about seeing it from the Moon.
poll: The Great Wall was worth all the work it took to build.

versions.title: The Great Wall
versions.text:
A long wall runs up and down hills. It is in China. It is the Great Wall. It is one of the biggest things we have built.

The Great Wall is not just one wall. It is lots of walls. They were built at different times. Work on them went on for more than two thousand years.

Long ago, men on fast horses came from the north. They took food. They took goods. So China built walls to protect its land. The first emperor of all China had his men join the walls.

At first, the walls were made of dirt and stone. Then men made the wall with brick. Most of the wall you see now is from five hundred years ago.

The wall has tall towers. Guards kept watch from them. Did they see a threat? Then they sent a signal. They made smoke in the day. They made fire at night.

Some say you can see the wall from the Moon. That is not true! The wall is long. But it is thin.

Now, lots of people go to see it each year.

A long stone wall winds up and down the hills of China. It is the Great Wall. It is one of the biggest things people have ever built.

The Great Wall is not just one wall. It is lots of walls. They were built at different times. People worked on them for more than two thousand years.

Long ago, men on fast horses came from the north. They took food and goods. So China built walls to protect its land. The first emperor of all China had his workers join lots of walls.

The first walls were made of packed dirt and stone. Later, workers made the wall with brick. Most of the wall you can visit now was built about five hundred years ago.

The wall has tall towers. Guards kept watch from the towers. If they saw men on horses, they sent a signal to the next tower. They made smoke in the day. They made fire at night.

Some people say you can see the wall from the Moon. That is not true! The wall is very long, but it is thin.

Now, lots and lots of people visit the Great Wall each year.

versions.title: The Great Wall

A long stone wall winds up and down the mountains of China like a giant snake. This is the Great Wall. It is one of the largest things people have ever built.

The Great Wall is not just one wall. It is many walls built at different times. People worked on these walls for more than two thousand years.

Long ago, groups of riders on fast horses came from the north. They attacked towns. They took food and goods. So rulers in China built walls to protect their land. The first emperor of all China had his workers join many short walls into one long line.

The first walls were made of packed dirt, stone, and wood. Later, builders used brick, which was stronger. Most of the wall people visit today was built about five hundred years ago.

The wall has tall watchtowers. Soldiers lived in the towers and kept watch. When they saw danger, they sent a signal to the next tower. They used smoke in the day and fire at night.

Some people say you can see the Great Wall from the Moon. That is not true! The wall is very long. But it is too thin to see from that far away.

Today, millions of people from around the world visit the Great Wall each year.

The Great Wall is not really one wall. It is many walls that were built and rebuilt at different times. People worked on these walls for more than two thousand years.

The earliest walls were made of packed dirt, stone, and wood. Later, builders used brick, which was stronger and lasted longer. Most of the wall that people visit today was built about five hundred years ago.

The wall has tall watchtowers. Soldiers lived in the towers and kept watch over the land. When they saw danger, they sent a signal to the next tower. They used smoke during the day and fire at night.

Today, millions of visitors from around the world walk on the Great Wall each year.

versions.title: The Great Wall of China
versions.text:
A long stone wall winds over the mountains and deserts of northern China like a giant snake. This is the Great Wall of China. It is one of the largest structures people have ever built.

The Great Wall is not really a single wall. It is a series of walls that were built, rebuilt, and joined over more than two thousand years. If you add all the parts together, they stretch over 21,000 kilometers.

Long ago, nomadic groups lived on the grasslands north of China. They moved from place to place with their animals, and they were skilled riders. Sometimes they would invade Chinese towns and carry off food and goods. To protect their land, Chinese rulers built walls along the border. Around 2,200 years ago, Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of all China, ordered workers to connect many older walls.

Each dynasty, or family of rulers, added to the wall. The early walls were made of packed earth, stone, and wood. The Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644, built most of the wall that visitors see today. Its workers used strong bricks and stone. They held them together with a mortar made of lime mixed with sticky rice. Soldiers, farmers, and prisoners did the hard, dangerous work.

The wall has thousands of watchtowers. Soldiers in the towers watched for danger. When they spotted an enemy, they sent a signal from tower to tower, using smoke by day and fire at night.

A popular myth says you can see the Great Wall from the Moon. This is not true. The wall is very long, but it is too narrow to see from so far away.

Today, the Great Wall is a World Heritage Site, and millions of people visit it each year.

versions.title: The Great Wall of China: A Wall of Many Ages
versions.text:
A massive stone wall winds across the mountains and deserts of northern China like an enormous serpent. This is the Great Wall of China, one of the most extensive structures human beings have ever constructed, and its history spans more than two thousand years.

The Great Wall is not actually a single wall. Instead, it is a vast fortification made up of many walls that were constructed, rebuilt, and connected by different rulers. If all of its sections were measured together, they would stretch over 21,000 kilometers.

Long ago, nomadic groups inhabited the grasslands beyond China's northern frontier, migrating with their herds. Because they were expert riders, they could travel rapidly, and occasionally they would invade Chinese villages and carry away food, livestock, and valuable goods. To defend their territory, Chinese rulers built barriers along the border. Around 2,200 years ago, Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, ordered laborers to connect numerous older walls.

Each dynasty, or ruling family, contributed to the wall, and while the earliest sections were made of compressed earth, stone, and wood, the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644, constructed most of the wall that visitors see today, using durable bricks and stone blocks bound together with a mortar made of lime mixed with sticky rice. Soldiers, farmers, and conscripted prisoners performed the exhausting and dangerous labor.

The wall includes thousands of watchtowers where soldiers observed the surrounding landscape. When they spotted an enemy, they transmitted a signal from tower to tower, using smoke by day and fire at night.

A popular misconception claims that the Great Wall is visible from the Moon. In reality, this is false, because although the wall is extremely long, it is far too narrow to distinguish from such an enormous distance.

versions.title: The Great Wall of China: A Wall of Many Ages
versions.text:
A massive stone wall winds across the mountains and deserts of northern China like an enormous serpent. This is the Great Wall of China, one of the most extensive structures human beings have ever constructed, and its complicated history spans more than two thousand years.

The Great Wall is not actually a single continuous wall. Instead, it is a vast fortification composed of numerous walls that were constructed, reconstructed, and connected by successive rulers. If all of its sections were measured together, they would stretch over 21,000 kilometers.

Long ago, nomadic peoples inhabited the grasslands beyond China's northern frontier, migrating seasonally with their herds. Because they were exceptionally skilled riders, they could travel rapidly, and occasionally they would invade Chinese settlements and carry away food, livestock, and valuable goods. To defend their territory, Chinese rulers erected barriers along the border. Around 2,200 years ago, Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, ordered laborers to connect numerous existing walls.

Each dynasty, or ruling family, contributed to the wall's development, and although the earliest sections consisted of compressed earth, stone, and timber, the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644, constructed most of the wall that visitors encounter today, using durable bricks and stone blocks bound together with a mortar made of lime combined with sticky rice. Soldiers, farmers, and conscripted prisoners performed the exhausting and frequently dangerous labor.

The wall incorporates thousands of watchtowers where soldiers observed the surrounding landscape. Whenever they detected an approaching enemy, they transmitted a signal from tower to tower, using smoke by day and fire at night.

A widespread misconception claims that the Great Wall is visible from the Moon. In reality, this is false, because although the wall is extraordinarily long, it is far too narrow to distinguish from such an enormous distance.

Today, the Great Wall is protected as a World Heritage Site, recognized as part of humanity's shared heritage, and millions of tourists visit it annually to appreciate its remarkable engineering, its dramatic scenery, and the extraordinary effort that its construction required.

versions.title: The Great Wall of China: A Wall of Many Ages
versions.text:
A massive stone wall winds across the mountains and deserts of northern China like an enormous serpent. This is the Great Wall of China, one of the most extensive structures human beings have ever constructed, and its complicated history spans more than two thousand years of construction, destruction, and renewal.

The Great Wall is not actually a single continuous wall. Instead, it is a vast fortification composed of numerous walls that were constructed, reconstructed, and connected by successive rulers. If all of its sections were measured together, including branches and parallel lines, they would stretch over 21,000 kilometers.

Long ago, nomadic peoples inhabited the grasslands beyond China's northern frontier, migrating seasonally with their herds. Because they were exceptionally skilled horsemen, they could travel rapidly across great distances, and occasionally they would invade Chinese settlements and carry away food, livestock, and valuable goods. To defend their territory, Chinese rulers erected barriers along the border. Around 2,200 years ago, Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, ordered laborers to connect numerous existing walls into a more continuous defensive line.

Each dynasty, or ruling family, contributed to the wall's development, and although the earliest sections consisted of compressed earth, stone, and timber, the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644, constructed most of the wall that visitors encounter today, using durable bricks and stone blocks bound together with a mortar made of lime combined with sticky rice. Soldiers, farmers, and conscripted prisoners performed the exhausting and frequently dangerous labor, often in remote and inhospitable locations.

The wall incorporates thousands of watchtowers where soldiers observed the surrounding landscape. Whenever they detected an approaching enemy, they transmitted a signal from tower to tower, using smoke by day and fire at night, so that reinforcements could be prepared quickly.

A widespread misconception claims that the Great Wall is visible from the Moon with the naked eye. In reality, this is false, because although the wall is extraordinarily long, it is far too narrow to distinguish from such an enormous distance.

Today, the Great Wall is protected as a World Heritage Site, recognized as part of humanity's shared heritage, and millions of tourists from every continent visit it annually to appreciate its remarkable engineering, its dramatic scenery, and the extraordinary human effort that its construction required.

versions.title: The Great Wall of China: A Wall of Many Ages
versions.text:
A massive stone wall winds across the mountains and deserts of northern China like an enormous serpent. This is the Great Wall of China, one of the most extensive structures human beings have ever constructed, and its complicated history encompasses more than two thousand years of construction, destruction, and renewal.

The Great Wall is not actually a single continuous barrier. Instead, it is a vast fortification composed of numerous walls that were constructed, reconstructed, and interconnected by successive rulers. If all of its sections were measured together, including branches and parallel lines, they would stretch over 21,000 kilometers.

Long ago, nomadic peoples inhabited the grasslands beyond China's northern frontier, migrating seasonally with their herds. Because they were exceptionally skilled horsemen capable of traveling rapidly across tremendous distances, they occasionally invaded Chinese settlements and carried away food, livestock, and valuable merchandise. To defend their territory, Chinese rulers erected barriers along the border, and approximately 2,200 years ago, Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, commanded laborers to connect numerous existing walls into a more continuous defensive line.

Each dynasty, or ruling family, contributed to the wall's development, and although the earliest sections consisted of compressed earth, stone, and timber, the Ming dynasty, which governed from 1368 to 1644, constructed most of the wall that visitors encounter today, utilizing durable bricks and stone blocks bound together with a mortar made of lime combined with sticky rice. Soldiers, agricultural workers, and conscripted prisoners performed the exhausting and frequently hazardous labor, often in remote and inhospitable locations.

The wall incorporates thousands of watchtowers from which soldiers observed the surrounding landscape. Whenever they detected an approaching enemy, they transmitted a signal from tower to tower, using smoke during daylight and fire after dark, so that military reinforcements could be prepared immediately.

A widespread misconception claims that the Great Wall is visible from the Moon with the unaided eye. In reality, this assertion is false, because although the wall is extraordinarily long, it is far too narrow to distinguish from such an enormous distance.

Today, the Great Wall is protected as a World Heritage Site, internationally recognized as part of humanity's shared cultural heritage, and millions of tourists from every continent visit it annually to appreciate its remarkable engineering, its dramatic mountainous scenery, and the extraordinary human determination that its construction required across many centuries.
